documents: Published paper: Gaubert-Bastide et al. (2022), Water Resources Research 58, e2021WR030680 (HAL deposit PDF, 21 pages including the HAL cover sheet)
pages_convention: printed journal pages ('n of 20'); the PDF page is the printed page + 1 because of the HAL cover sheet. Supporting Information was not supplied; S-figures are cited through the main-text page that reports them.

entry.evidence: Here we show that high-resolution seismic noise interferometry can be obtained for monitoring hydrological variations.

steps.action: Report earlier piezometer and temperature studies of basin 5-2 (Réfloch 2018): southward natural flow, stronger feeding of the southern part, and a barrier that vanishes within 1-2 days.
steps.quote: the hydraulic barrier created below the basin disappears in a maximum of 1–2 days

steps.action: Pose the problem that too few piezometers, especially in the east, prevent detailed mapping of the hydraulic dome and its evolution in a heterogeneous aquifer.
steps.quote: [...] work suffers from the small number of piezometers especially on the eastern part of the basin

steps.action: Recall the authors' preliminary 10-sensor, 10-day noise study, which suggested strong lateral variability of the dome.
steps.quote: showed strong lateral variability of the hydraulic dome

steps.action: Deploy a dense network of 99 three-component 4.5 Hz nodes around basin 5-2, covering many azimuths and distances, recording at 250 Hz for 19 days.
steps.quote: In all, 99 seismic nodes were deployed around the infiltration basin 5-2.

steps.action: Set the hydrological conditions in the field: 5 days with an empty basin as baseline, then two controlled filling and drainage cycles, with basin level and piezometer P95 recorded.
steps.quote: two cycles of filling/emptying of the basin 5-2 were performed to determine the efficiency of the seismic monitoring methodology

steps.action: Estimate the average infiltration velocity in the vadose zone from the time shifts between basin-level peaks and water-table peaks, finding a faster rate in the second cycle.
steps.quote: we could estimate a 0.3 m/hr infiltration velocity during the first infilling whereas it rises to 0.5 m/hr during the second infilling

steps.action: Check the premise of the noise-correlation method (stable, isotropic sources) by double beamforming of the horizontal components in 2-5 Hz over 24-hr windows, noting a westward ring-road dominance on weekdays.
steps.quote: The beamforming outputs appear stable over time and show almost isotropic patterns at 400 m/s velocity

steps.action: Build the cross-correlation workflow: rotate to radial and transverse components, whiten daily in 1-20 Hz, normalize 1-min windows, and stack the TT, RR and ZZ correlations over 10 min or 1 hr.
steps.quote: these cross-correlations are stacked over 10 mn or 1 hour, to improve the signal-to-noise ratio

steps.action: Gather 4,851 averaged correlations by distance and characterize the wavefield: TT is dominated by a Love wave, RR is slightly faster, and ZZ is complex; energy is limited to roughly 2-10 Hz.
steps.quote: The TT component is dominated by a surface wave with an apparent velocity slightly over 400 m/s

steps.action: Use the symmetry of the distance-sorted correlations as a second check of the isotropic-source premise.
steps.quote: They are all symmetric, which reinforces the hypothesis of the isotropic spatial distribution [...] .

steps.action: Estimate hourly δv/v for all 4,851 pairs by stretching the ballistic Love wave against the mean reference, rejecting correlation coefficients below 0.8 (26.7% of values) and shifting δv/v to zero at t = 0.
steps.quote: This analysis is performed with the stretching technique (Sens-Schönfelder & Wegler, 2006)

steps.action: Compare δv/v for two basin-crossing pairs (R2-R21, R15-R30) with the P95 water table: they are anti-correlated, with discrepancies before filling, between the two maxima and at the end.
steps.quote: The δv/v and water table curves are anti-correlated: negative velocity variations are associated with rising water table.

steps.action: Invoke the authors' earlier poroelastic fluid-substitution modeling as the expectation that explains the anti-correlation.
steps.quote: quantitatively well explained using a poroelastic fluid substitution approach (Garambois et al., 2019)

steps.action: State two rival sources of the discrepancies: path-integrated δv/v versus a local piezometer reading, and δv/v sensitivity to saturation changes in the unsaturated zone.
steps.quote: These discrepancies might come from two reasons.

steps.action: Design the discriminating step: a high-resolution tomography that removes the path-integration ambiguity before discussing the unsaturated zone.
steps.quote: In order to prevent any ambiguous interpretation, we aim at implementing a tomography process with very high spatial resolution

steps.action: Vary the frequency band for pair R2-R21 (Figure S2a, Supporting Information) and find hydrological δv/v only between 2 and 5.5 Hz.
steps.quote: This frequency analysis confirms that velocity variations related to hydrological cycles are observed only in a very limited frequency band

steps.action: Compute Love-wave depth sensitivity kernels (Figure S2b) to obtain the expected depth range of sensitivity in 2-5 Hz.
steps.quote: the sensitivity of Love waves to changes in the environment is maximum between 2 and 7 m depth

steps.action: Invert δv/v paths into 2-D maps with straight-ray tomography (Barmin 2001, as adapted by Mordret 2014): Gaussian smoothing, 19.9 m cells, iterative rejection of high-RMS rays, three iterations.
steps.quote: we use the (straight) ray theory approach of Barmin et al. (2001), to carry out fast and reliable tomography

steps.action: Check tomographic resolution and parameter choice with checkerboard tests and several parameter attempts; also check that RMS rejection removes no particular azimuth.
steps.quote: additional tests carried out with the help of checkerboard tests have confirmed the great resolution of the tomography with this illumination

steps.action: Repeat the inversion for every hour of the 455-hr experiment (RMS 9.2-18.8%, 1,940-4,851 rays) to produce dynamic δv/v maps.
steps.quote: A similar inversion procedure is carried out for each hour of the monitoring experiment

steps.action: Read the map sequence: a negative δv/v dome builds from 124 hr, peaks at 225 hr, follows both cycles, and does not return to equilibrium at 455 hr, unlike the piezometer.
steps.quote: Surprisingly, although decreasing, the system does not return to equilibrium at the end of the experiment (at 455 hr)

steps.action: Derive 3-D views and horizontal gradients at the two peaks (225 and 390 hr), showing an elongated dome, a steeper southern slope, a hyper-localized eastern response and a strong gradient in the western dyke.
steps.quote: What stands out from Figure 9 is the elongation of the dome along the stretch of the basin.

steps.action: Compare δv/v extracted at tomography cells near piezometers P95 and S20, smoothed over 10 hr, with the measured water table through time.
steps.quote: During the first infilling, both signals follow a similar increasing trend and reach a maximum at the same time.

steps.action: Use the second filling cycle as a repeat event to check that the timing and intensity of the response recur.
steps.quote: A similar trend is observed during the second infilling.

steps.action: Plot water table against δv/v (H-plots) and compare with the inherited 1% = 1 m relation: it holds roughly during the first infilling only.
steps.quote: the proportionality relationship between the changes in the velocity and the water table variations roughly fits that proposed by Voisin et al. (2017)

steps.action: Establish a hysteresis between infilling and drainage at both P95 and S20, with a nested secondary loop at S20 near the dyke.
steps.quote: Both Figures 10d and 10e present a well-identified hysteretic behavior

steps.action: Convert the residual 2% δv/v at water-table return into a water-content change through the poroelastic fluid-substitution model, assuming 35% porosity.
steps.quote: the observed remaining 2% of δv/v would correspond to water content variations of about 30%–35%

steps.action: Retain delayed drainage of the unsaturated zone (gravity, capillarity, relative permeability, possibly double porosity) as the explanation for the slow δv/v recovery and the hysteresis.
steps.quote: the slow rate of seismic velocity change could be due to the slower decrease of the water content within the desaturated zone

steps.action: Compare a NW-SE piezometer transect with tomography cells at six times: both show a dome, but tomography gives steeper slopes, a maximum shifted southeast, and persistent dyke effects.
steps.quote: The tomography reveals that the dome has steeper slopes than those obtained by interpolation of the piezometric levels

steps.action: Conclude that the dense passive network characterizes hourly, high-resolution dome dynamics and is sensitive to both water-table and unsaturated-zone changes; limits stated are frequency band and depth.
steps.quote: We have demonstrated the sensitivity of the surface waves velocity to groundwater changes.

tree.answer: Yes: a hydraulic dome under the infiltration basin, produced by controlled filling, and its δv/v signature
Only locally, by sparse piezometers; spatial field inferred from δv/v tomography
Characterize the capability of a dense passive network to map water-table and water-content changes
Two rival causes of δv/v-piezometer mismatch: path integration versus unsaturated-zone sensitivity
Partly: cell-level tomography removes path integration; poroelastic model gives water content; predictions only qualitative
Set: two controlled basin filling and drainage cycles in the field
Yes: beamforming and symmetry premise checks, frequency variation, checkerboard tests, second cycle, piezometer comparisons
Capability kept; unsaturated-zone delayed drainage retained as best explanation

end.claim: A dense passive seismic network with ballistic Love-wave δv/v tomography maps the hourly 3-D evolution of a controlled hydraulic dome at high resolution, and is sensitive to both water-table and unsaturated-zone water-content changes.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the dense 99-node three-component deployment, which gives 4,851 raypaths with full azimuthal coverage, neither the tomography nor the cell-level comparison with piezometers would exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the network was designed to improve resolution of a dome expected from the preliminary 10-sensor study (p. 3), but no stated hypothesis directed the acquisition. Claim: δv/v could have failed to track piezometers at P95 and S20, or along the transect (pp. 9, 13, 16), and checkerboard tests could have shown poor resolution (p. 10). The unsaturated-zone interpretation was not put to a test that could fail. Registration: tomography parameters were chosen 'after different attempts' (p. 10); nothing is reported as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Green's function retrieval from correlations of diffuse fields (Lobkis & Weaver 2001; Derode et al. 2003, J. Acoust. Soc. Am.)
Double beamforming to locate noise sources (Boué et al. 2013 code)
Distributed acoustic sensing on buried or dark fibers, proposed for future dense monitoring

novelty_claims.quote: Here we show that high-resolution seismic noise interferometry can be obtained for monitoring hydrological variations.
We were also able to show that it is possible to detect residual variations within the unsaturated zone, above the piezometric water level.

limits: Only the published paper was supplied: no review file, and no Supporting Information, so Figures S1-S2, the dispersion analysis and Movie S3 were not seen. Their steps are coded from the main-text descriptions. Checkerboard results are asserted but not shown. Mapped δv/v uncertainty is given only as inversion RMS; no per-cell resolution or uncertainty is reported. The controlled basin cycles were coded F on mode hypothesis by analogy with laboratory conditions, though their stated purpose is to test the method (inference). The path-integration rival (step 14) is never explicitly rejected; the coder infers it is weakened because hysteresis persists at cell level after tomography. Sub-claims and their statuses: the unsaturated-zone delayed-drainage explanation is best_explanation, not confirmed, as the authors defer it to future laboratory experiments (p. 18). The dome geometry (elongation, steeper southern slope, southeast-shifted maximum) is estimate_with_resolution, with resolution stated only qualitatively. The 1% = 1 m relation is regularity_in_range, holding only during the first infilling. The 30-35% water-content figure rests on an assumed 35% porosity and a fluid-substitution model, with no uncertainty given. Generalization to other MAR systems and DAS (pp. 17-18) is proposed, not tested.

disagreements.target: Earlier ballistic-wave water-table monitoring (Voisin et al. 2017; Garambois et al. 2019; Kim & Lekic 2019)
disagreements.support: The hysteresis between δv/v and water table, and the residual δv/v after the water table returns, are attributed to unsaturated-zone water content, which those studies ignored.
disagreements.quote: they simply considered water table changes, without taking into account potential variations occurring within the unsaturated zone

disagreements.target: Linear 1% δv/v = 1 m water-table relation (Voisin et al. 2017; Garambois et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: H-plots at P95 and S20 show the relation roughly holds during the first infilling, but drainage phases follow a different, slower path.
disagreements.quote: the velocity variations decrease is much slower than the water table with −1% still remaining [...]

disagreements.target: Piezometer-based picture of the hydraulic dome (Réfloch 2018; interpolation of piezometric levels)
disagreements.support: Transect comparison at six times shows the tomography gives steeper dome slopes and a maximum shifted tens of meters southeast of P95, where no piezometer exists.
disagreements.quote: The tomography reveals that the dome has steeper slopes than those obtained by interpolation of the piezometric levels

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Coda waves (the usual basis of δv/v monitoring)
alternatives_considered.reason: Ballistic surface waves dominate seismograms in sedimentary settings, where coda has low energy because of weak scattering.
Satisfactory signal-to-noise ratio, a simple symmetric wavefield, and stable horizontal noise sources; RR and ZZ are disturbed, possibly by pump noise.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Lower (<2 Hz) and higher (>5.5 Hz) frequencies
alternatives_considered.reason: Hydrological δv/v appears only in this band, and kernels show sensitivity concentrated at 2-7 m depth.
Improve the signal-to-noise ratio without degrading the dynamics; shorter windows risk noisier time variations.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Correlation length 50 m, smoothing strength 0.05, three iterations of RMS rejection
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Different attempts (unspecified parameter values); more iterations
alternatives_considered.reason: Compromise between resolution and stability, checked with checkerboard tests; stop at three iterations to keep at least 40% of rays.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Sensitivity to water saturation in the unsaturated zone (delayed drainage)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Path integration of δv/v versus local piezometer measurement
alternatives_considered.reason: Tomography localizes δv/v at cells near piezometers; the poroelastic model links the residual δv/v to water content.
